title: The Lesson I Learned From the Unused Talent
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From the Unused Talent
The most dangerous thing you can lose may not be your money, your opportunity, or even your reputation. It may be the gift God placed inside you that never gets used.
There is a tragedy that rarely makes headlines.
It does not happen when someone fails.
It happens when someone never even tries.
Most people imagine their greatest regret will be something they did.
Jesus taught that the greater tragedy may be something they never did.
A gift never shared.
A calling never answered.
A dream buried beneath fear.
A talent hidden beneath excuses.
A life spent protecting what God intended to multiply.

Many years ago, I read the Parable of the Talents and assumed it was primarily about stewardship, productivity, and responsibility. Those lessons are certainly there. But the older I become, the more I realize that this story reaches far deeper into the human soul.
Because buried inside this parable is a terrifying question:
What if the thing standing between you and God's purpose is not rebellion?
What if it is fear?
Jesus tells the story in Matthew 25:14-30. A master prepares for a journey and entrusts his servants with varying amounts of talents.

The Greek word used is τάλαντον (talanton), originally referring to a large measure of weight and, by extension, a significant amount of money. The point was not the exact amount. The point was trust.
The master trusted them.
One servant received five talents.
Another received two.
Another received one.
The servants with five and two immediately put their talents to work and gained more.
But the servant with one talent did something different.
He dug a hole.
He buried it.
He hid it.
And when the master returned, he proudly presented exactly what he had been given.
Nothing lost.
Nothing gained.
Perfectly preserved.
Completely wasted.
His explanation reveals the real issue.
"I knew thee that thou art an hard man..." (Matthew 25:24 KJV)
The Greek text says:
ἔγνων σε ὅτι σκληρὸς εἶ ἄνθρωπος
"I knew you to be a hard man."
Notice what happened.
His actions flowed from his perception.
He misunderstood the character of his master.
And that misunderstanding shaped his entire life.
The servant was not condemned because he stole.
Not because he squandered.
Not because he rebelled.
He was condemned because fear convinced him to do nothing.
That should stop every believer in their tracks.
Because many followers of Christ are not living in open rebellion.
They simply keep burying what God entrusted to them.
Some bury their testimony.
Some bury their calling.
Some bury their gifts.
Some bury their compassion.
Some bury their creativity.
Some bury their influence.
Some bury their ministry.
Some bury their voice.
Not because they hate God.
Because they are afraid.
Afraid of criticism.
Afraid of failure.
Afraid of rejection.
Afraid of embarrassment.
Afraid of making mistakes.
Afraid of what others might think.
So they dig a hole.
And they wait.
The tragedy is that buried talents never bless anyone.
Imagine if Noah had buried obedience.
Imagine if Moses had buried leadership.
Imagine if David had buried courage.
Imagine if Esther had buried influence.
Imagine if Peter had buried his voice after denying Christ.
Imagine if Paul had buried his testimony because of his past.
Imagine if Mary Magdalene had buried her story because of shame.
The Kingdom of God would have looked very different.
And maybe that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us know exactly what God has placed in our hands.
We know.
We just keep postponing obedience.
The enemy rarely needs to destroy a calling.
He only needs to delay it long enough.
One year becomes five.
Five years becomes ten.
A decade becomes a lifetime.
Then someday we stand before God holding exactly what He gave us.
Untouched.
Unused.
Unmultiplied.
Yet the beauty of the Gospel is that Jesus specializes in rescuing buried things.
That is the story of Scripture.
Again and again.
Humanity buries what God wants to use.
God redeems it anyway.
The Bible's grand story is not about flawless people achieving greatness.
It is about a holy Savior redeeming scandalized sinners.
The Hebrew word often translated "grace" is חֵן (chen), meaning favor, kindness, acceptance freely given.
The Greek New Testament uses χάρις (charis).
Grace.
Undeserved favor.
Unmerited kindness.
God giving what we could never earn.
And nowhere is that grace more visible than at the Cross.
Humanity buried the Son of God.
Rejected Him.
Mocked Him.
Scourged Him.
Crucified Him.
Placed Him in a tomb.
Yet what looked like history's greatest scandal became history's greatest victory.
What looked buried was actually being prepared for resurrection.
What looked finished was only beginning.
What looked defeated was conquering death itself.
This is why our message remains the same:
The Cross proves that God can redeem what appears lost.
The empty tomb proves that buried things can rise again.
Maybe your talent has been hidden for years.
Maybe your calling has been buried beneath disappointment.
Maybe your faith has been buried beneath wounds.
Maybe your purpose has been buried beneath fear.
Maybe your voice has been buried beneath shame.
Hear this clearly:
Jesus still raises buried things.
The same Christ who walked out of the grave can resurrect gifts you thought were gone forever.
The same Savior who restored Peter can restore you.
The same Lord who transformed Saul into Paul can transform your story.
The same grace that redeemed scandal can redeem wasted years.
You are not reading these words by accident.
Perhaps the Holy Spirit is gently uncovering something you buried long ago.
Perhaps this is your invitation to stop digging deeper holes and start walking in obedience.
Not tomorrow.
Today.
Because talents were never meant to be protected.
They were meant to be invested for God's glory.
And when we faithfully use what God has entrusted to us, we participate in something larger than ourselves.
We become part of His Kingdom work.
We become part of His redemptive story.
We become living testimonies that Jesus still transforms lives.
If this message exposed something you have buried, be honest.
Let that comment become a declaration before God and a testimony before others.
They may be carrying a gift the world desperately needs.
Not for popularity.
For ministry.
You never know whose buried calling may be uncovered because you chose to share truth.
If your desire is truly to glorify God, one practical way to participate is by helping spread His truth through sharing, supporting, and partnering with this mission.
One day you will stand before God with everything He placed in your hands.
May that day not be marked by what you protected.
May it be marked by what you surrendered.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having too little.
It is leaving too much buried.
And the greatest miracle is that Jesus still calls buried things back to life.
